title: The Call Stack, Activation Records and Depth
quickIdea: Every live call owns one frame. The stack is as deep as the recursion tree is tall, not as busy as it is: a function that makes a million calls one level deep uses a constant number of frames.
remember: Each call pushes an activation record holding its parameters, its locals, the return address and saved registers; the record is popped when that call returns.

The space a recursion uses is the maximum number of frames alive at once, times the frame size. For a linear recursion that is O(n); for naive Fibonacci, which makes exponentially many calls, it is still O(n), because the two branches run one after the other.
GATE CSE 2005 Q.81(a) is exactly this question. In foo(n) the loop calls foo(i) for i = 0..n-1, one after another, so the deepest chain is foo(n), foo(n-1), ..., foo(0): n+1 frames, answer O(n).

The number of calls and the depth are different numbers. get(6) in GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.39 is invoked 25 times, but no more than 7 frames are ever alive, because each branch finishes before its sibling starts.
A frame's locals keep their values while the frame is alive, which is what makes the reversed output of GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.19 possible: each frame still holds its own character.

The stack region is fixed at run time. Deep or unbounded recursion exhausts it and the program aborts; that is a runtime event, not a compile-time error, and the C standard says nothing about when it happens.

example.prompt: double foo(int n) { int i; double sum; if (n == 0) return 1.0; sum = 0.0; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += foo(i); return sum; } What is the space complexity of foo?
example.work: foo(n) calls foo(n-1) first; that call returns before foo(n-2) begins, so siblings are never alive together. The deepest chain is n+1 frames. Each frame holds one int, one double and the return address, a constant number of objects.
example.answer: O(n) space, although the number of calls is exponential in n.

gateAngle: Space questions are phrased as 'the space complexity of the above code'. Answer with the depth, not the call count, and say so explicitly: 2005 Q.81(a) offers O(1), O(n), O(n!) and n^n, and only O(n) follows from the maximum depth.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2005 Q.81(a): the space complexity of the recursive foo above.
variations.why: Sequential sibling calls give a depth of n+1 frames whatever the number of calls.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: What is the space complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci int fib(int n) { return n < 2 ? n : fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); }?
variations.answer: O(n): the two calls are sequential, so the stack holds at most n frames even though 2F(n+1)-1 calls are made.
variations.why: The same separation as 2005 Q.81(a), with the count and the depth differing by an exponential factor.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why does a recursion with two calls per level not need twice the stack of a recursion with one?
variations.answer: Because the calls are made one after the other. The first returns and its frame is popped before the second is pushed, so the peak is the depth of a single path, not the width of the tree.
variations.why: The intuition that a wider tree costs more stack is the most common wrong answer on space questions.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A function recurses on n/2 with a base case at n <= 1. How many frames are alive at the deepest point?
variations.answer: floor(log2 n) + 1, which is O(log n).
variations.why: Halving gives logarithmic depth, and depth is what the stack measures.

trap.what: Reading the number of recursive calls as the stack depth.
trap.why: The stack holds the frames on one root-to-leaf path at a time. Branches that run sequentially share the same frames, so a call tree with millions of nodes can be only a few dozen levels tall.
trap.counterexample: fib(30) makes 2 692 537 calls with the formula 2F(31)-1, and its stack is never deeper than 30 frames.

check.question: void get(int n) { if (n < 1) return; get(n-1); get(n-3); } How many frames are alive at most during get(6)?
check.answer: Seven - the chain get(6), get(5), get(4), get(3), get(2), get(1), get(0).
check.explanation: The first recursive call always drives straight down to a base case before any second call is made, so the deepest path is the decreasing chain, and its length is n+1.
